reading.body:
AI assistance in enterprise resource planning is now embedded directly inside the systems that run payroll, procurement, supply chains, and financial ledgers, meaning errors or data exposures propagate through the same authoritative records the business relies on.

Three of the four vendors listed are headquartered in the United States, with SAP based in Germany. That split matters for data governance because ERP systems hold personally identifiable employee data, financial records, and supplier contracts, and the jurisdiction of the vendor shapes which regulatory frameworks govern how AI processes that data. The data does not say where customer data is hosted or processed, so no stronger claim about regulatory exposure can be made from it.

The risk notes attached to two tools are worth reading carefully. SAP Joule carries a ledger-modification risk notation, meaning the AI copilot has proximity to accounting records that, once altered, affect audit trails. Workday AI carries a sensitive HR data exposure notation. These are not risks unique to AI, but embedding AI agents into systems that previously required deliberate human navigation of permissions and workflows compresses the distance between a model output and a consequential write operation. The data does not cover compute infrastructure, power draw, or data center footprint for any of these deployments, so no connection to grid or building constraints can be drawn here.
